blocks.text: Amides contain the functional group -CONH2. Because they can be made from carboxylic acids they are sometimes called acid amides. They are made by reacting acyl chlorides with ammonia or primary amines at room temperature, releasing white fumes of hydrogen chloride:

items: CH3COCl + NH3 -> CH3CONH2 + HCl (ethanamide); C6H5COCl + NH3 -> C6H5CONH2 + HCl (benzamide).
CH3COCl + CH3CH2NH2 -> CH3CONHCH2CH3 + HCl (N-ethylethanamide); CH3COCl + C6H5NH2 -> CH3CONHC6H5 + HCl (N-phenylethanamide).
The HCl formed reacts with another molecule of ammonia or amine to form a salt (NH3 + HCl -> NH4+ Cl-; RNH2 + HCl -> RNH3+ Cl-), so an excess of ammonia or amine is used to complete the reaction.

blocks.title: Physical properties
blocks.text: All amides except methanamide, a liquid, are solids with sharp melting points, and they have quite high boiling points because of strong hydrogen bonding between molecules. In N-substituted amides the melting and boiling points fall as the number of alkyl substituents increases, because there are fewer N-H hydrogens for hydrogen bonding.

Amides are much weaker bases than aliphatic amines; unlike amines, they form neutral solutions in water. They show resonance: the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised towards the oxygen of the carbonyl group (R-CO-NH2 <-> R-C(O-)=NH2+), which makes the electrons on nitrogen less available and so decreases the basicity. The partial double-bond character between carbon and nitrogen also makes the amide C-N bond (132 pm) shorter than an ordinary C-N single bond (147 pm).

Amides are the least reactive acid derivatives, because the nitrogen lone pair, delocalised over the carbonyl oxygen, reduces the partial positive charge (electrophilic power) of the carbonyl carbon. Their reactions are slow and need prolonged heating or a catalyst (acid or base).

items: Acid hydrolysis gives the carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt: CH3CONH2 + H2O + HCl -> CH3COOH + NH4Cl.
Base-catalysed hydrolysis gives the salt of the acid and ammonia: CH3CONH2 + NaOH -> CH3COONa + NH3; the free acid is obtained with dilute HCl: CH3COONa + HCl -> CH3COOH + NaCl.
Reduction with lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III) in dry ethoxyethane (ether) gives primary amines: CH3CONH2 + 4[H] -> CH3CH2NH2 + H2O; C6H5CONH2 + 4[H] -> C6H5CH2NH2 + H2O (phenylmethanamine).

Middle left: R-CO-NH2 with curly arrows moving the N lone pair towards C and the C=O electrons onto O, giving R-C(O-)=NH2+. Middle right: amide C-N 132 pm against amine C-N 147 pm. Bottom: acid and alkaline hydrolysis of ethanamide and its reduction by LiAlH4 to ethanamine.
blocks.caption: Making amides, their low basicity and their reactions (original diagram after the book's equations).
blocks.long_description: Amides form when ammonia or an amine attacks an acyl chloride. In the amide the nitrogen lone pair is shared with the C=O group: this makes amides neutral rather than basic, shortens the C-N bond, and makes the carbonyl carbon less open to attack, so amide reactions are slow.
